V. I MPLEMENTATION
We leverage io uring to implement AisLSM with RocksDB
(Section V-A). We also comprehensively consider multiple
aspects to optimize and enhance AisLSM (Section V-B).
A. Implementation of AisLSM
Overview. We take RocksDB to prototype AisLSM while
the ideas of AisLSM can be applied to other LSM-tree vari-
ants. Doing asynchronous I/Os to revolutionize the procedure
of compaction is orthogonal to other optimization techniques
proposed to enhance LSM-tree. We mainly make use of the
iouring to implement AisLSM’s asynchronous writes and
fsync s. Overall, the core functions of AisLSM add or change
about 1,624 lines of code (LOC) in RocksDB version 7.10.0.
Compaction procedure. AisLSM follows RocksDB to 1)
flush an immutable memtable as an L0SST file, 2) maintain
background threads for flush and compaction jobs, and 3) cal-
culate scores to choose an overfilled level and input SST fileswith key ranges overlapped for compaction. Figure 7 illus-
trates eight main steps with which AisLSM does with an com-
paction. In these steps, AisLSM uses the io uring’s structures
such as uring_queue to collect data for each SST file. It
calls io uring’s interfaces such as io_uring_prep_fsync
andio_uring_submit to prepare an asynchronous fsync
and submit an I/O request, respectively.
Deferred check-up and deletion. At the beginning of a
compaction, AisLSM checks if input parental SST files are
already durable ( 8). If so, it removes grandparental SST
files by inserting them into a collection vector that RocksDB
has managed for the purpose of deleting files. The check-up
does not cost much time. For example, in dealing with the
aforementioned test of putting 80GB of KV pairs, AisLSM
spent overall 749.1 seconds, out of which all check-up actions
cost about 0.01 ms. Such a time cost is negligible.
Version and state tracking. RocksDB has a Manifest file
with an in-memory Version to record the change of SST
files (see Figure 1). As AisLSM decouples the visibility and
durability for LnSST file ( n≥1), it tracks and updates the
state of each LnSST file in the Manifest file and Version.
B. Optimizations and Complements
Concurrent compactions. AisLSM maintains background
threads to do flush and compaction jobs. It makes com-
putations of current compaction thread execute on a CPU
core while a kernel thread of io uring is simultaneously
handling I/Os with storage for prior compaction, without
blocking the user-space compaction thread. Today multi-core
and many-core CPUs have gathered momentum. NVMe SSD
also contains numerous hardware queues for parallel I/O
streams [21, 36] while Linux kernel has blk-mq with multiple
software queues [20, 40]. AisLSM supports multiple threads or
instances concurrently conducting compaction jobs. Its asyn-
chronous I/O model, when deployed on multiple compaction
threads, can exploit the parallelism capabilities of both CPU
and storage for effectual concurrent executions.
I/O polling. NVMe SSD embraces much shorter access
latency than SATA SSDs. Many researchers have used the I/O
polling mechanism, instead of conventional I/O interrupts, to
interact with NVMe SSD [20, 21, 35]–[37]. In implementing
AisLSM, we also consider I/O polling with NVMe SSD
and io uring. Note that the joint setup of I/O polling and
iouring currently works only when a file is opened with the
ODIRECT flag, i.e., in the direct I/O mode [38].
Failed I/Os. I/O errors might take place over time. When an
I/O operation fails, the conventional synchronous I/O model
helps LSM-tree handle the error in a timely fashion. As
AisLSM waits for the completion signals of all asynchronous
file writes, any I/O error occurring at these writes can be
swiftly detected and processed like with conventional LSM-
tree. AisLSM defers the check-up of asynchronous fsync ,
so detecting and handling I/O errors for fsync are also
postponed. However, even if an I/O error happens in persisting
an SST file, the durability of KV pairs stored in the file is not
impaired since AisLSM has retained parental SST files untilthe check-up. Searching KV pairs in this file is also unaffected
since file system accommodates KV pairs in the OS’s buffer
cache or storage device’s disk cache. AisLSM explicitly calls
fsync for a retry to fix the I/O error. In the worst case, it
regenerates and replaces that problematic file.
Outlier SST files. In unusual cases, some SST files, once
generated in a compaction, hardly participate in subsequent
compactions, because the key ranges they cover might not
be frequently used (i.e., outliers). AisLSM still ensures the
durability of such inactive outlier SST files. This is the other
reason why AisLSM submits one request for all SST files
generated in a compaction to schedule a compound asyn-
chronous fsync . As long as any one of them is to be involved
in a future compaction, AisLSM checks if the asynchronous
fsync has been done for all relevant SST files. By doing
so, AisLSM avoids overlooking outliers. This also helps to
delete their parental SST files. In addition, there might be a
very low likelihood that outliers form a batch and have no
opportunity to be compacted again. AisLSM has tracked all
SST files asynchronously persisted with io uring. It schedules
a specific check-up in off-peak hours for such outliers.
VI. E VALUATION
A. Evaluation Setup
Platform. The machine used for evaluation is an HP Z2
G4 workstation. It is with an Intel Core i9-9900K CPU
and 64GB DRAM as main memory. The OS is Ubuntu
22.04.1 with Linux kernel 6.2.7 installed on an HDD (Western
WD20EZWX-60F5KA0 in 2TB). There are two additional
SSDs in the machine. One is an SATA SSD (Samsung 870
EVO in 1TB) and the other one is an NVMe SSD (SK
Hynix HFS512GD9TNGL2A0A in 480GB). The latter is used
as the main storage device to hold data for all LSM-tree
variants throughout following experiments. The compiler is
GCC/G++ version 9.5.0. The version of io uring (liburing) is
2.3. Because XFS and io uring have been jointly optimized
for efficient use of asynchronous I/Os [41, 42], we mainly use
XFS except for NobLSM that needs a customized Ext4.
Benchmarks. One benchmark we use is the db bench
micro-benchmark built in RocksDB. It can synthesize contin-
uous Put or Get requests in typical access patterns. The other
one is the YCSB macro-benchmark emulating a suite of real-
world workloads [43]. On finishing a workload, they report
the throughput (MB/s) or execution time that we utilize as the
metrics to measure and compare performances for LSM-trees.
Competitors. Besides the vanilla RocksDB [3], we choose
a few state-of-the-art LSM-tree variants that represent different
approaches researchers have explored to improve performance
for LSM-tree. They are ADOC [16], TRIAD [19], Rocks-
bu [31], SILK [12], PhotonDB [32] and NobLSM [26]. All
of them except NobLSM are open-source, implemented with
RocksDB. As to NobLSM built atop LevelDB, we implement
it by modifying RocksDB and Ext4 for a fair comparison. Be-
low we briefly summarize the characteristics of these variants.
ADOC. ADOC monitors the data flow among multiple
components of LSM-tree. Accordingly, it adjusts the numberof threads and size of SSTable to control processing rate and
schedule the frequency of background jobs, thereby in turn
controlling the data flow within LSM-tree to reduce stalls.
TRIAD. Firstly, TRIAD tries to separate hot KV pairs
that are frequently updated from cold ones at the memtable.
Secondly, TRIAD postpones a compaction until the overlap
between key ranges of SST files aggregates to some extent.
Thirdly, it makes use of WAL to play the role of L0SST file,
instead of writing the same KV pairs again. TRIAD attempts
to alleviate write amplification with these techniques.
Rocks-bu. Rocks-bu is the other RocksDB variant that we
have found being with the use of io uring. A team of three
practitioners made use of the batch I/O feature of io uring to
group I/O requests for RocksDB.
SILK. SILK focuses on I/O scheduling between insertions
with memtable, flushes, and compactions, mainly for shorter
tail latency. It allocates more bandwidth to internal operations,
i.e., flushes and compactions, when foreground service is not
heavy. It gives higher priority to flushes and compactions at
lower levels (e.g., L0→L1). Moreover, it allows compactions
at lower levels to preempt ones at higher levels.
PhotonDB. A group of Alibaba’s researchers engineered
PhotonDB by using io uring and coroutines to subsume
threads in RocksDB [44]. Although they have been aware
of asynchronous I/Os provided by io uring, they focus on
applying coroutines and io uring to serve multiple clients in a
network database. With a single client carrying one or multiple
foreground threads, PhotonDB still waits for the completion
of I/Os with io uring in the conventional synchronous manner.
NobLSM. NobLSM employs the periodical asynchronous
commit of Ext4 journaling to persist files and thus remove
fsync s out of the critical path of compaction. It relies on
Ext4 and demands handcrafted changes into Linux kernel.
B. Micro-benchmark
We employ db bench to issue four typical workloads. In
particular, with each LSM-tree variant, we perform following
workloads in order: fillrandom (random insertion of KV pair),
overwrite (random update of KV pair), readseq (sequential
retrieval of KV pair), and readrandom (random retrieval of
KV pair). For each workload, we fix an overall quantity of
data volume and follow the default uniform distribution to
generate requests. We designate four foreground threads. Each
thread puts (resp. gets) 20GB of KV pairs for write (resp. read)
requests. We set the key size as 16B while varying the value
size to be 64B, 128B, 256B, 512B, 1KB, 2KB, and 4KB. The
reason we use 80GB of data is twofold. Firstly, such a volume
of data concretely entails continual compactions with massive
CPU computations and disk I/Os over time. Secondly, the
NVMe SSD we are running on has 480GB raw capacity. We
must consider LSM-tree’s write amplifications that can occupy
multiple times of 80GB [13, 19, 27, 45]–[47]. We also take
into account that due to a composition of LSM-tree variants,
workloads, value sizes, and rounds, overwhelming data may
frequently trigger SSD’s internal modules like garbage collec-tion and wear leveling that impact performance results [48]–
[50]. We choose a volume of 80GB to alleviate such impact.
Figure 8a to Figure 8d capture the bandwidth of each LSM-
tree variant with four workloads. Let us analyze the results
in three aspects. Firstly, using its asynchronous I/O model
to revolutionize compaction, AisLSM significantly boosts the
performance of RocksDB. For example, with fillrandom and
seven increasing value sizes, the throughput of AisLSM is
1.3×, 1.4×, 1.6×, 1.8×, 2.0×, 2.1×, and 2.14 ×that of
RocksDB. As AisLSM offloads file write and fsync I/Os
to kernel threads and makes compaction thread focus on CPU
computations, it is able to quickly complete a compaction job
and soon initiate the next one, thereby gaining high through-
put. We have further recorded the stall time for AisLSM.
As mentioned in Section III, RocksDB spent 1,399.9 seconds
in finishing fillrandom with 1KB values while stalls lasted
for 1,179.1 seconds. For AisLSM, the total execution time
and stall time are 749.1 and 618.1 seconds, respectively. This
comparison further justifies that the removal of synchronous
I/Os from the critical path of compaction effectually reduces
the stall time and in turn boosts performance for LSM-tree.
In addition, given a fixed size of SST file (64MB), AisLSM
achieves higher performance with larger values. A larger value
size means fewer KV pairs to be fitted in an SST file. LSM-tree
starts off a compaction regarding the capacity of each level, or
measured in the practical unit, the number of SST files. With
the same number of SST files for compaction, fewer KV pairs
evidently need less time on merge-sorting keys and other CPU
computations. As a result, AisLSM finishes a compaction in
a more prompt pace for larger KV pairs.
Secondly, AisLSM significantly outperforms state-of-the-
art prior works. For example, with overwrite workload and
1KB values, the throughput of AisLSM is 1.8 ×, 2.0×, 2.9×,
1.9×, 2.3×, 1.6×, and 1.4 ×that of original RocksDB, ADOC,
TRIAD, Rocks-bu, SILK, PhotonDB and NobLSM, respec-
tively. These LSM-tree variants have undertaken different
approaches to optimize LSM-tree, mainly on reducing the
performance penalty caused by compactions. ADOC and SILK
take into account the processing capability of storage device
and attempt to schedule compaction jobs with threads. Simi-
larly, one main technique of TRIAD is to postpone scheduling
compactions until it has to do so due to too many overlapped
keys. Whereas, they place emphasis on scheduling at the
granularity of compaction jobs but fail to realize the critical
serial order of CPU computations and storage I/Os in a com-
paction. Consequently, their compaction thread stays waiting
for I/O completion signals from kernel thread while CPU core
does not simultaneously work on meaningful computations.
Given a mass of KV pairs that are continuously arriving to
stress LSM-tree, the effect of scheduling compaction jobs is
inferior and unsatisfactory. As to PhotonDB and Rocks-bu, a
replacement over conventional concepts or interfaces without
an in-depth study to locate concrete performance bottlenecks
is unlikely to bring about substantial gains. Let us still take
overwrite and 1KB value size for example. With coroutine and
iouring, PhotonDB produces a marginal improvement over641282565121K2K4K

of io uring’s batch I/O only even degrades performance by

NobLSM is inferior to AisLSM with both fillrandom and
overwrite workloads. The most significant gap between them
is 1.53 ×with fillrandom and 4KB values. The reason is
twofold. Firstly, NobLSM does not consider scheduling file
write I/Os but still conducts them synchronously. Whereas,
AisLSM asynchronously deals with both file write and fsync
I/Os. Secondly, the time cost of checking if SST files are
asynchronously committed is non-trivial, particularly with fast
NVMe SSD. For each compaction, NobLSM submits all
output SST files for tracking with one customized system call
and later asks Ext4 to check for every file, resulting in multiple
system calls. NobLSM employs a global kernel-space table
to record and track SST files. It is time-consuming to insert
and query each file with the table, especially when many SST
files gradually accumulate due to continuous compactions.
Comparatively, for one asynchronous fsync , AisLSM both
submits a request and collects the result by calling respective
iouring interfaces only once. In addition, AisLSM does not
rely on any file system or handcrafted Linux kernel, which
is a stark contrast to NobLSM. To sum up, AisLSM is much
more effectual and portable than NobLSM.
Thirdly, although LSM-tree is generally used to serve write-
intensive workloads, we have tested AisLSM’s capability in
serving read requests. As shown Figure 8c and Figure 8d,
AisLSM is comparable to RocksDB and NobLSM, while some
LSM-tree variants exhibit dramatically low performance. For
example, the throughputs of TRIAD and PhotonDB are just
15.2% and 13.5% of AisLSM’s, respectively, with readrandom
and 1KB values. The change AisLSM incurs to read procedure
is just to load KV pairs from a transiently non-durable SST
file. This, however, does not affect the visibility of data or
the actions of locating a specific key. AisLSM thus achieves a
well balance between write and read performances while, for
instance, TRIAD keeps too many files at L0with overlapped
key ranges that are not friendly to searches [19, 51]–[53].
C. Deep Dissection with AisLSM
We have done various experiments to deeply evaluate
AisLSM. We validate if it guarantees crash consistency (Sec-
tion VI-C1). We test if it ensures the accessibility of KV pairs(Section VI-C2). As AisLSM shortens the critical path of com-
paction, we measure how much it reduces the user-facing tail
latency (Section VI-C3). Regarding implementation and opti-
mization techniques AisLSM contains, we further analyze the
contribution from each of them and figure out the root cause of
performance boost for AisLSM (Section VI-C4). We next test
if AisLSM works on another platform (Section VI-C5), with
multiple compaction threads (Section VI-C6), and multiple
instances (Section VI-C7).
1) Crash Consistency Test: To test the crash consistency of
AisLSM, we use the command ‘ halt -f -p -n ’ to sud-
denly power off Linux when writing KV pairs with db bench’s
fillrandom [26]. We repeat this test for five times successively
with RocksDB and AisLSM. We find that, besides KV pairs
being appended to WAL, ones residing in SST files are
recoverable and retrievable for both RocksDB and AisLSM.
By default, they do not persist WALs with fsync s. The main
difference between them is that AisLSM does not wait for
the durability of output SST files per compaction. It also does
not immediately delete input SST files. AisLSM flushes L0
SST files to persist all KV pairs received from users. Only
after check-up will it delete SST files used as input for past
compactions. By tracking the generation dependency between
SST files, AisLSM guarantees any KV pair sinking down from
LntoLn+1(n≥0) is traceable and durable. All these jointly
enable AisLSM’s crash recoverability.
2) Data Accessibility Test: We measure whether AisLSM
manages to find out all KV pairs under search. To do so,
we first run fillrandom by engaging a foreground thread in
putting down KV pairs in 20GB with various value sizes
and then search keys with readrandom. We note that newer
RocksDB since version 6.2 no longer guarantees that db bench
always searches for a stored key. Instead, db bench randomly
generates target keys and some of them might not be existent
in the LSM-tree. The randomization is based on a seed related
to the search time by default. RocksDB provides an option
to fix the seed so that we can repeat the same readrandom
test case. Under equivalent search conditions, AisLSM and
RocksDB locate the same number of KV pairs, with about
63.2% of all searched keys found. This justifies that AisLSM’s
data accessibility is identical to that of RocksDB.

substantially boost performance compared to RocksDB. This

highest leap (1.5 ×) over RocksDB occurs at 512B value size.

one compaction thread by default. We varied the number of

throughput than RocksDB. This confirms that AisLSM well
supports multi-threading concurrent compactions.

for both p2KVS (RocksDB) and AisLSM and engaged each

overwrite workloads. Figure 11a and Figure 11b comparatively
present the throughputs of AisLSM and p2KVS on handling
two workloads, respectively. AisLSM has evident advantage
over p2KVS on both workloads. For example, with 1KB
values, AisLSM yields 1.5 ×higher throughput than p2KVS.
AisLSM differs from p2KVS in that an instance of the former
is more performant than an instance of RocksDB used by the
latter. Given identical strategies for sharding and scheduling
KV pairs among multiple instances, an instance of AisLSM
processes requests at a much more prompt pace than p2KV .
AisLSM is hence more efficient than p2KVS. As to overwrite,
AisLSM outperforms p2KVS in all value sizes. The highest
gap between them is 2.0 ×with 4KB values.
D. Macro-benchmark
The Yahoo! Cloud Serving Benchmark (YCSB) [43] is
a comprehensive, open-source tool that is widely used to
evaluate the performance of LSM-tree-based KV stores. YCSB
provides six core workloads that emulate access patterns found
in typical production environments. They are A (update heavy,
50%/50% read/write), B (read mostly, 95%/5% read/write), C
(read only, 100% read), D (read latest, 95%/5% read/insert),
E (short ranges, 95%/5% range query/insert), and F (read-
modify-write, 50%/50% read-modify-write/read). These work-
loads are either write- or read-dominant, or a mix of write and
read requests. YCSB’s default size per KV pair is about 1KB.
We run YCSB workloads in the order of Load-A, A, B, C, F,
D, Load-E and E by referring to previous works [25, 26, 56].
We make Load-A and Load-E remove existing data in each
LSM-tree variant and put down 50 million of KV pairs. They
hence store roughly 50GB of data as the base. Every workload
carries ten million of requests to be served. Figure 12a to
Figure 12h capture the service time for each LSM-tree in
such an order. Note that for AisLSM we show the results forall its three variants mentioned in Section VI-C4. From these
diagrams we can obtain four observations.
Firstly, with write-dominant workloads, such as Load-A and
Load-E, AisLSM variants consistently yield higher perfor-
mance than state-of-the-art LSM-tree variants. For example,
with Load-A, the time RocksDB, ADOC, TRIAD, Rocks-bu,
SILK, PhotonDB, and NobLSM spent is 1.8 ×, 1.8×, 2.5×,
1.8×, 2.3×, 2.2×, and 1.1 ×that of AisLSM, respectively.
This improvement is again accredited to the novel compaction
procedure revolutionized by AisLSM with asynchronous I/O
model. The shortened time cost of compaction entails less
stall time, thereby processing workloads with less service
time. Secondly, as to read-dominant workloads, including
workloads B, C, D, and E, AisLSM family yields comparable
or higher performance than state-of-the-art LSM-tree variants.
For example, with workload B, the service time of RocksDB,
ADOC, TRIAD, Rocks-bu, SILK, PhotonDB, and NobLSM
is 1.4×, 1.1×, 3.5×, 1.2×, 1.2×, 1.9×and 1.2 ×that of
AisLSM, respectively. These results aligns with what we
have obtained with db bench’s readrandom. As illustrated
by Figure 8d, TRIAD and PhotonDB have shown the lowest
throughputs. Thirdly, for a workload mixed with write and
read requests, such as workloads A and F, AisLSM is still
performant over other LSM-tree variants. For example, to
finish these two workloads, original RocksDB demands 19.1%
and 17.2% more time than AisLSM, respectively. Last but not
the least, AisLSM-interrupt, which is a variant of AisLSM
with interrupt-driven I/Os, is a bit faster than AisLSM in
handling workloads with read requests. For example, with
workload E for range queries, AisLSM-interrupt working in
the buffered I/O mode cost 4.9% less time than AisLSM
working in the direct I/O mode. As mentioned, although the
access speed of NVMe SSD is higher than legacy storage
devices, the use of OS’s or LSM-tree’s buffers would be
helpful to serve read requests.

# B. Optimizations and Complements

**Summary:** The partial document discusses the design and evaluation of AisLSM, a system that optimizes the compaction process in LSM-trees by leveraging asynchronous I/O operations. Key points covered include:

1. **Compaction Process**: AisLSM uses io_uring structures to handle asynchronous I/O operations, such as file writes and fsyncs, to improve the efficiency of compaction in LSM-trees.

2. **Deferred Check-up and Deletion**: AisLSM checks the durability of SST files at the beginning of compaction and defers the deletion of grandparental SST files, ensuring data durability with minimal time cost.

3. **Version and State Tracking**: The system tracks changes in SST files using a Manifest file and an in-memory Version, decoupling visibility and durability for SST files.

4. **Concurrent Compactions**: AisLSM supports concurrent compaction jobs using multiple threads, exploiting the parallelism capabilities of modern CPUs and storage devices like NVMe SSDs.

5. **I/O Polling**: The system uses I/O polling with NVMe SSDs to reduce latency, working in direct I/O mode for efficient data handling.

6. **Handling Failed I/Os**: AisLSM detects and processes I/O errors swiftly, ensuring data durability and retrying failed operations.

7. **Outlier SST Files**: The system manages inactive SST files by scheduling asynchronous fsyncs and check-ups during off-peak hours to maintain data integrity.

8. **Evaluation**: The document describes the evaluation setup, including the hardware platform and benchmarks used to test AisLSM against other LSM-tree variants. AisLSM demonstrates significant performance improvements in throughput and reduced tail latency compared to state-of-the-art designs.

Overall, AisLSM enhances LSM-tree performance by optimizing the compaction process through asynchronous I/O operations and efficient resource utilization.

with key ranges overlapped for compaction. Figure 7 illus-
trates eight main steps with which AisLSM does with an com-
paction. In these steps, AisLSM uses the io uring’s structures
such as uring_queue to collect data for each SST file. It
calls io uring’s interfaces such as io_uring_prep_fsync
andio_uring_submit to prepare an asynchronous fsync
and submit an I/O request, respectively.
Deferred check-up and deletion. At the beginning of a
compaction, AisLSM checks if input parental SST files are
already durable ( 8). If so, it removes grandparental SST
files by inserting them into a collection vector that RocksDB
has managed for the purpose of deleting files. The check-up
does not cost much time. For example, in dealing with the
aforementioned test of putting 80GB of KV pairs, AisLSM
spent overall 749.1 seconds, out of which all check-up actions
cost about 0.01 ms. Such a time cost is negligible.
Version and state tracking. RocksDB has a Manifest file
with an in-memory Version to record the change of SST
files (see Figure 1). As AisLSM decouples the visibility and
durability for LnSST file ( n≥1), it tracks and updates the
state of each LnSST file in the Manifest file and Version.
B. Optimizations and Complements
Concurrent compactions. AisLSM maintains background
threads to do flush and compaction jobs. It makes com-
putations of current compaction thread execute on a CPU
core while a kernel thread of io uring is simultaneously
handling I/Os with storage for prior compaction, without
blocking the user-space compaction thread. Today multi-core
and many-core CPUs have gathered momentum. NVMe SSD
also contains numerous hardware queues for parallel I/O
streams [21, 36] while Linux kernel has blk-mq with multiple
software queues [20, 40]. AisLSM supports multiple threads or
instances concurrently conducting compaction jobs. Its asyn-
chronous I/O model, when deployed on multiple compaction
threads, can exploit the parallelism capabilities of both CPU
and storage for effectual concurrent executions.
I/O polling. NVMe SSD embraces much shorter access
latency than SATA SSDs. Many researchers have used the I/O
polling mechanism, instead of conventional I/O interrupts, to
interact with NVMe SSD [20, 21, 35]–[37]. In implementing
AisLSM, we also consider I/O polling with NVMe SSD
and io uring. Note that the joint setup of I/O polling and
iouring currently works only when a file is opened with the
ODIRECT flag, i.e., in the direct I/O mode [38].
Failed I/Os. I/O errors might take place over time. When an
I/O operation fails, the conventional synchronous I/O model
helps LSM-tree handle the error in a timely fashion. As
AisLSM waits for the completion signals of all asynchronous
file writes, any I/O error occurring at these writes can be
swiftly detected and processed like with conventional LSM-
tree. AisLSM defers the check-up of asynchronous fsync ,
so detecting and handling I/O errors for fsync are also
postponed. However, even if an I/O error happens in persisting
an SST file, the durability of KV pairs stored in the file is not
impaired since AisLSM has retained parental SST files untilthe check-up. Searching KV pairs in this file is also unaffected
since file system accommodates KV pairs in the OS’s buffer
cache or storage device’s disk cache. AisLSM explicitly calls
fsync for a retry to fix the I/O error. In the worst case, it
regenerates and replaces that problematic file.
Outlier SST files. In unusual cases, some SST files, once
generated in a compaction, hardly participate in subsequent
compactions, because the key ranges they cover might not
be frequently used (i.e., outliers). AisLSM still ensures the
durability of such inactive outlier SST files. This is the other
reason why AisLSM submits one request for all SST files
generated in a compaction to schedule a compound asyn-
chronous fsync . As long as any one of them is to be involved
in a future compaction, AisLSM checks if the asynchronous
fsync has been done for all relevant SST files. By doing
so, AisLSM avoids overlooking outliers. This also helps to
delete their parental SST files. In addition, there might be a
very low likelihood that outliers form a batch and have no
opportunity to be compacted again. AisLSM has tracked all
SST files asynchronously persisted with io uring. It schedules
a specific check-up in off-peak hours for such outliers.
VI. E VALUATION
A. Evaluation Setup
Platform. The machine used for evaluation is an HP Z2
G4 workstation. It is with an Intel Core i9-9900K CPU
and 64GB DRAM as main memory. The OS is Ubuntu
22.04.1 with Linux kernel 6.2.7 installed on an HDD (Western
WD20EZWX-60F5KA0 in 2TB). There are two additional
SSDs in the machine. One is an SATA SSD (Samsung 870
EVO in 1TB) and the other one is an NVMe SSD (SK
Hynix HFS512GD9TNGL2A0A in 480GB). The latter is used
as the main storage device to hold data for all LSM-tree
variants throughout following experiments. The compiler is
GCC/G++ version 9.5.0. The version of io uring (liburing) is
2.3. Because XFS and io uring have been jointly optimized
for efficient use of asynchronous I/Os [41, 42], we mainly use
XFS except for NobLSM that needs a customized Ext4.
Benchmarks. One benchmark we use is the db bench
micro-benchmark built in RocksDB. It can synthesize contin-
uous Put or Get requests in typical access patterns. The other
one is the YCSB macro-benchmark emulating a suite of real-
world workloads [43]. On finishing a workload, they report
the throughput (MB/s) or execution time that we utilize as the
metrics to measure and compare performances for LSM-trees.
Competitors. Besides the vanilla RocksDB [3], we choose
a few state-of-the-art LSM-tree variants that represent different
approaches researchers have explored to improve performance
for LSM-tree. They are ADOC [16], TRIAD [19], Rocks-
bu [31], SILK [12], PhotonDB [32] and NobLSM [26]. All
of them except NobLSM are open-source, implemented with
RocksDB. As to NobLSM built atop LevelDB, we implement
it by modifying RocksDB and Ext4 for a fair comparison. Be-
low we briefly summarize the characteristics of these variants.
ADOC. ADOC monitors the data flow among multiple
components of LSM-tree. Accordingly, it adjusts the numberof threads and size of SSTable to control processing rate and
schedule the frequency of background jobs, thereby in turn
controlling the data flow within LSM-tree to reduce stalls.
TRIAD. Firstly, TRIAD tries to separate hot KV pairs
that are frequently updated from cold ones at the memtable.
Secondly, TRIAD postpones a compaction until the overlap
between key ranges of SST files aggregates to some extent.
Thirdly, it makes use of WAL to play the role of L0SST file,
instead of writing the same KV pairs again. TRIAD attempts
to alleviate write amplification with these techniques.
Rocks-bu. Rocks-bu is the other RocksDB variant that we
have found being with the use of io uring. A team of three
practitioners made use of the batch I/O feature of io uring to
group I/O requests for RocksDB.
SILK. SILK focuses on I/O scheduling between insertions
with memtable, flushes, and compactions, mainly for shorter
tail latency. It allocates more bandwidth to internal operations,
i.e., flushes and compactions, when foreground service is not
heavy. It gives higher priority to flushes and compactions at
lower levels (e.g., L0→L1). Moreover, it allows compactions
at lower levels to preempt ones at higher levels.
PhotonDB. A group of Alibaba’s researchers engineered
PhotonDB by using io uring and coroutines to subsume
threads in RocksDB [44]. Although they have been aware
of asynchronous I/Os provided by io uring, they focus on
applying coroutines and io uring to serve multiple clients in a
network database. With a single client carrying one or multiple
foreground threads, PhotonDB still waits for the completion
of I/Os with io uring in the conventional synchronous manner.
NobLSM. NobLSM employs the periodical asynchronous
commit of Ext4 journaling to persist files and thus remove
fsync s out of the critical path of compaction. It relies on
Ext4 and demands handcrafted changes into Linux kernel.
B. Micro-benchmark
We employ db bench to issue four typical workloads. In
particular, with each LSM-tree variant, we perform following
workloads in order: fillrandom (random insertion of KV pair),
overwrite (random update of KV pair), readseq (sequential
retrieval of KV pair), and readrandom (random retrieval of
KV pair). For each workload, we fix an overall quantity of
data volume and follow the default uniform distribution to
generate requests. We designate four foreground threads. Each
thread puts (resp. gets) 20GB of KV pairs for write (resp. read)
requests. We set the key size as 16B while varying the value
size to be 64B, 128B, 256B, 512B, 1KB, 2KB, and 4KB. The
reason we use 80GB of data is twofold. Firstly, such a volume
of data concretely entails continual compactions with massive
CPU computations and disk I/Os over time. Secondly, the
NVMe SSD we are running on has 480GB raw capacity. We
must consider LSM-tree’s write amplifications that can occupy
multiple times of 80GB [13, 19, 27, 45]–[47]. We also take
into account that due to a composition of LSM-tree variants,
workloads, value sizes, and rounds, overwhelming data may
frequently trigger SSD’s internal modules like garbage collec-tion and wear leveling that impact performance results [48]–
[50]. We choose a volume of 80GB to alleviate such impact.
Figure 8a to Figure 8d capture the bandwidth of each LSM-
tree variant with four workloads. Let us analyze the results
in three aspects. Firstly, using its asynchronous I/O model
to revolutionize compaction, AisLSM significantly boosts the
performance of RocksDB. For example, with fillrandom and
seven increasing value sizes, the throughput of AisLSM is
1.3×, 1.4×, 1.6×, 1.8×, 2.0×, 2.1×, and 2.14 ×that of
RocksDB. As AisLSM offloads file write and fsync I/Os
to kernel threads and makes compaction thread focus on CPU
computations, it is able to quickly complete a compaction job
and soon initiate the next one, thereby gaining high through-
put. We have further recorded the stall time for AisLSM.
As mentioned in Section III, RocksDB spent 1,399.9 seconds
in finishing fillrandom with 1KB values while stalls lasted
for 1,179.1 seconds. For AisLSM, the total execution time
and stall time are 749.1 and 618.1 seconds, respectively. This
comparison further justifies that the removal of synchronous
I/Os from the critical path of compaction effectually reduces
the stall time and in turn boosts performance for LSM-tree.
In addition, given a fixed size of SST file (64MB), AisLSM
achieves higher performance with larger values. A larger value
size means fewer KV pairs to be fitted in an SST file. LSM-tree
starts off a compaction regarding the capacity of each level, or
measured in the practical unit, the number of SST files. With
the same number of SST files for compaction, fewer KV pairs
evidently need less time on merge-sorting keys and other CPU
computations. As a result, AisLSM finishes a compaction in
a more prompt pace for larger KV pairs.
Secondly, AisLSM significantly outperforms state-of-the-
art prior works. For example, with overwrite workload and
1KB values, the throughput of AisLSM is 1.8 ×, 2.0×, 2.9×,
1.9×, 2.3×, 1.6×, and 1.4 ×that of original RocksDB, ADOC,
TRIAD, Rocks-bu, SILK, PhotonDB and NobLSM, respec-
tively. These LSM-tree variants have undertaken different
approaches to optimize LSM-tree, mainly on reducing the
performance penalty caused by compactions. ADOC and SILK
take into account the processing capability of storage device
and attempt to schedule compaction jobs with threads. Simi-
larly, one main technique of TRIAD is to postpone scheduling
compactions until it has to do so due to too many overlapped
keys. Whereas, they place emphasis on scheduling at the
granularity of compaction jobs but fail to realize the critical
serial order of CPU computations and storage I/Os in a com-
paction. Consequently, their compaction thread stays waiting
for I/O completion signals from kernel thread while CPU core
does not simultaneously work on meaningful computations.
Given a mass of KV pairs that are continuously arriving to
stress LSM-tree, the effect of scheduling compaction jobs is
inferior and unsatisfactory. As to PhotonDB and Rocks-bu, a
replacement over conventional concepts or interfaces without
an in-depth study to locate concrete performance bottlenecks
is unlikely to bring about substantial gains. Let us still take

NobLSM is inferior to AisLSM with both fillrandom and
overwrite workloads. The most significant gap between them
is 1.53 ×with fillrandom and 4KB values. The reason is
twofold. Firstly, NobLSM does not consider scheduling file
write I/Os but still conducts them synchronously. Whereas,
AisLSM asynchronously deals with both file write and fsync
I/Os. Secondly, the time cost of checking if SST files are
asynchronously committed is non-trivial, particularly with fast
NVMe SSD. For each compaction, NobLSM submits all
output SST files for tracking with one customized system call
and later asks Ext4 to check for every file, resulting in multiple
system calls. NobLSM employs a global kernel-space table
to record and track SST files. It is time-consuming to insert
and query each file with the table, especially when many SST
files gradually accumulate due to continuous compactions.
Comparatively, for one asynchronous fsync , AisLSM both
submits a request and collects the result by calling respective
iouring interfaces only once. In addition, AisLSM does not
rely on any file system or handcrafted Linux kernel, which
is a stark contrast to NobLSM. To sum up, AisLSM is much
more effectual and portable than NobLSM.
Thirdly, although LSM-tree is generally used to serve write-
intensive workloads, we have tested AisLSM’s capability in
serving read requests. As shown Figure 8c and Figure 8d,
AisLSM is comparable to RocksDB and NobLSM, while some
LSM-tree variants exhibit dramatically low performance. For
example, the throughputs of TRIAD and PhotonDB are just
15.2% and 13.5% of AisLSM’s, respectively, with readrandom
and 1KB values. The change AisLSM incurs to read procedure
is just to load KV pairs from a transiently non-durable SST
file. This, however, does not affect the visibility of data or
the actions of locating a specific key. AisLSM thus achieves a
well balance between write and read performances while, for
instance, TRIAD keeps too many files at L0with overlapped
key ranges that are not friendly to searches [19, 51]–[53].
C. Deep Dissection with AisLSM
We have done various experiments to deeply evaluate
AisLSM. We validate if it guarantees crash consistency (Sec-
tion VI-C1). We test if it ensures the accessibility of KV pairs(Section VI-C2). As AisLSM shortens the critical path of com-
paction, we measure how much it reduces the user-facing tail
latency (Section VI-C3). Regarding implementation and opti-
mization techniques AisLSM contains, we further analyze the
contribution from each of them and figure out the root cause of
performance boost for AisLSM (Section VI-C4). We next test
if AisLSM works on another platform (Section VI-C5), with
multiple compaction threads (Section VI-C6), and multiple
instances (Section VI-C7).
1) Crash Consistency Test: To test the crash consistency of
AisLSM, we use the command ‘ halt -f -p -n ’ to sud-
denly power off Linux when writing KV pairs with db bench’s
fillrandom [26]. We repeat this test for five times successively
with RocksDB and AisLSM. We find that, besides KV pairs
being appended to WAL, ones residing in SST files are
recoverable and retrievable for both RocksDB and AisLSM.
By default, they do not persist WALs with fsync s. The main
difference between them is that AisLSM does not wait for
the durability of output SST files per compaction. It also does
not immediately delete input SST files. AisLSM flushes L0
SST files to persist all KV pairs received from users. Only
after check-up will it delete SST files used as input for past
compactions. By tracking the generation dependency between
SST files, AisLSM guarantees any KV pair sinking down from
LntoLn+1(n≥0) is traceable and durable. All these jointly
enable AisLSM’s crash recoverability.
2) Data Accessibility Test: We measure whether AisLSM
manages to find out all KV pairs under search. To do so,
we first run fillrandom by engaging a foreground thread in
putting down KV pairs in 20GB with various value sizes
and then search keys with readrandom. We note that newer
RocksDB since version 6.2 no longer guarantees that db bench
always searches for a stored key. Instead, db bench randomly
generates target keys and some of them might not be existent
in the LSM-tree. The randomization is based on a seed related
to the search time by default. RocksDB provides an option
to fix the seed so that we can repeat the same readrandom
test case. Under equivalent search conditions, AisLSM and
RocksDB locate the same number of KV pairs, with about
63.2% of all searched keys found. This justifies that AisLSM’s
data accessibility is identical to that of RocksDB.

Given a shorter latency to finish a compaction, AisLSM is able
to process more compaction jobs and incur fewer stalls.

polling: We have configured and tested three variants for
AisLSM in order to thoroughly figure out the root cause of
performance gain. The first one relies on io uring to only
conduct asynchronous fsync s for each compaction. The
second one does asynchronous I/Os with io uring for both
file writes and fsync s, but all I/Os are interrupt-driven. The
third one is the full version that has been used for comparison
in Section VI-B. It is similar to the second one except being
tuned with the I/O polling and direct I/O mode for NVMe
SSD. The three variants are thereafter referred to as AisLSM-

substantially boost performance compared to RocksDB. This
aligns with our observation in Section III, as synchronous
fsync s cost longer time than file writes (see Figure 4).

two workloads, respectively. AisLSM has evident advantage
over p2KVS on both workloads. For example, with 1KB
values, AisLSM yields 1.5 ×higher throughput than p2KVS.
AisLSM differs from p2KVS in that an instance of the former
is more performant than an instance of RocksDB used by the
latter. Given identical strategies for sharding and scheduling

processes requests at a much more prompt pace than p2KV .
AisLSM is hence more efficient than p2KVS. As to overwrite,

D. Macro-benchmark
The Yahoo! Cloud Serving Benchmark (YCSB) [43] is
a comprehensive, open-source tool that is widely used to
evaluate the performance of LSM-tree-based KV stores. YCSB
provides six core workloads that emulate access patterns found
in typical production environments. They are A (update heavy,
50%/50% read/write), B (read mostly, 95%/5% read/write), C
(read only, 100% read), D (read latest, 95%/5% read/insert),
E (short ranges, 95%/5% range query/insert), and F (read-
modify-write, 50%/50% read-modify-write/read). These work-
loads are either write- or read-dominant, or a mix of write and
read requests. YCSB’s default size per KV pair is about 1KB.
We run YCSB workloads in the order of Load-A, A, B, C, F,
D, Load-E and E by referring to previous works [25, 26, 56].
We make Load-A and Load-E remove existing data in each
LSM-tree variant and put down 50 million of KV pairs. They
hence store roughly 50GB of data as the base. Every workload
carries ten million of requests to be served. Figure 12a to
Figure 12h capture the service time for each LSM-tree in
such an order. Note that for AisLSM we show the results forall its three variants mentioned in Section VI-C4. From these
diagrams we can obtain four observations.
Firstly, with write-dominant workloads, such as Load-A and
Load-E, AisLSM variants consistently yield higher perfor-
mance than state-of-the-art LSM-tree variants. For example,
with Load-A, the time RocksDB, ADOC, TRIAD, Rocks-bu,
SILK, PhotonDB, and NobLSM spent is 1.8 ×, 1.8×, 2.5×,
1.8×, 2.3×, 2.2×, and 1.1 ×that of AisLSM, respectively.
This improvement is again accredited to the novel compaction
procedure revolutionized by AisLSM with asynchronous I/O
model. The shortened time cost of compaction entails less
stall time, thereby processing workloads with less service
time. Secondly, as to read-dominant workloads, including
workloads B, C, D, and E, AisLSM family yields comparable
or higher performance than state-of-the-art LSM-tree variants.
For example, with workload B, the service time of RocksDB,
ADOC, TRIAD, Rocks-bu, SILK, PhotonDB, and NobLSM
is 1.4×, 1.1×, 3.5×, 1.2×, 1.2×, 1.9×and 1.2 ×that of
AisLSM, respectively. These results aligns with what we
have obtained with db bench’s readrandom. As illustrated
by Figure 8d, TRIAD and PhotonDB have shown the lowest
throughputs. Thirdly, for a workload mixed with write and
read requests, such as workloads A and F, AisLSM is still
performant over other LSM-tree variants. For example, to
finish these two workloads, original RocksDB demands 19.1%
and 17.2% more time than AisLSM, respectively. Last but not
the least, AisLSM-interrupt, which is a variant of AisLSM
with interrupt-driven I/Os, is a bit faster than AisLSM in
handling workloads with read requests. For example, with
workload E for range queries, AisLSM-interrupt working in
the buffered I/O mode cost 4.9% less time than AisLSM
working in the direct I/O mode. As mentioned, although the
access speed of NVMe SSD is higher than legacy storage
devices, the use of OS’s or LSM-tree’s buffers would be
helpful to serve read requests.

workloads under three distributions, i.e., Zipfian, uniform, and
latest. Because of space limitation, we present the execution
time with workloads A and F, as both of them contain a
50%/50% mix of write and read requests. As indicated by Fig-
ure 13, AisLSM outperforms other LSM-tree variants under
Zipfian and uniform distributions. With the latest distribution,
AisLSM achieves a comparable performance than RocksDB.
The reason is that, the latest distribution always chooses the
most recent data for operation. Write and read requests are
hence mostly satisfied at LSM-tree’s memtables and block
cache. With regard to frequent merges upon updating the
same keys repeatedly at the memtable level, compactions are
not largely triggered. The performance gain of revolutionized
compaction is consequently marginal for AisLSM.
VII. R ELATED WORKS
We have quantitatively discussed and evaluated a few prior
works in Section VI. Some techniques of them have been
proved to be useful to reduce the performance penalty caused
by compactions. For example, the way TRIAD separates hot
and cold KV pairs was also considered by other works. Huang
et al. [27] found that even a small number of frequently
updated hot KV pairs would quickly fill up SST files and cause
more compaction jobs over time. They accordingly install an
auxiliary log to distinguish and handle hot data. Decoupling
values from keys is another technique that can effectively
lower the frequency of compactions, since a pointer (location)
of each actual value, instead of the entire value, is stored in
SST file [19, 28, 29]. Some researchers proposed concurrent
compactions [14, 30, 57]. For example, p2KVS [30] mentioned
in Section VI-C7 partitions KV space into independent spaces
and manages multiple instances correspondingly. Such in-
stances concurrently schedule and perform compaction jobs.
There are also research works that leverage buffers to acceler-
ate search performance for LSM-tree [51, 55]. AisLSM’s rev-
olutionized compaction is complementary to these techniques
and they can collaboratively take effect for high performance.
Foregoing designs mainly attempt at the granularity of
compaction jobs. Some researchers considered dissecting the
internals of a compaction. For example, Zhang et al. [17]
tried to make use of the parallelism between CPU and I/O
device, like what we have done in this paper. However, they
decomposed a compaction job in the granularity of blocks(4KB by default). Then they tried to pipeline CPU computation
and synchronous I/Os for consecutive blocks of every SST
file. Limited by the perspective at the block-level granularity
and obliviousness of asynchronous I/Os, they had to rely
on multiple parallel storage devices for high I/O bandwidth
to catch up the computing speed of CPU. Whereas, this
demands changes across user- and kernel-spaces for storage
management. Additionally, their pipeline might not be stable
over time, since small data in one or few blocks is difficult
for CPU and storage to process at a steadily stable speed.
Comparatively, AisLSM takes effect at the granularity of SST
file in scores of megabytes and exploits existing storage stack
(e.g., io uring and NVMe SSD) for implementation. It shall
have higher performance, viability, and stability.
Not many researchers considered the impact of fsync s
used in compactions on the performance of LSM-tree [25, 26].
Prior to aforementioned NobLSM, Kim et al. [25] proposed
BoLT. BoLT produces one huge output SST file for each
compaction and persists all compacted KV pars in one aggre-
gated fsync . This reduces the performance penalty caused by
multiple fsync calls on individual SST files, but the eventual
large fsync still synchronously occurs on the critical path.
Researchers also studied the processing speeds for compu-
tations and I/Os for compaction. Some of them used FPGA
to accelerate computations [58, 59]. The emerging storage
devices like NVMe SSD and persistent memory (pmem) also
attracted wide attention [20, 47, 60]. For example, Chen et
al. [20] proposed SpanDB that jointly makes use of faster
NVMe SSD and ordinary slower SSD to suit the characteristics
of WAL and SST files for storage. It also uses I/O polling
with NVMe SSD. In addition, SpanDB and p2KVS share
similarity in dedicating separate foreground and background
threads to serve user requests and do flush or compaction
jobs, respectively. By doing so, SpanDB aims to overlap fore-
ground services with background jobs at runtime. Meanwhile,
researchers developed LSM-tree variants [6, 7, 13, 14, 29, 61]
to leverage the non-volatility and byte-addressability of pmem.
Though, the winding down of Intel’s Optane DC memory
business [62, 63] may impact the deployment of them.
VIII. C ONCLUSION
In this paper, we overhaul the compaction procedure of
LSM-tree. The critical path of a compaction job is composed
of CPU computations and disk I/Os. At runtime, LSM-tree’s
compaction thread synchronously waits for the completion of
file write and fsync I/Os that a kernel thread is handling. We
accordingly develop AisLSM that overlaps CPU computations
(resp. user thread) with disk I/Os (resp. kernel thread) for
consecutive compactions and, particularly, performs disk I/Os
with an asynchronous model. AisLSM also decouples the
visibility from durability for compacted KV pairs. With a
deferred check-up and deletion strategy, AisLSM ensures that
data stored in SST files is visible and durable. We thoroughly
evaluate AisLSM. Experiments show that, by shortening the
critical path of compaction, AisLSM highly boosts the perfor-
mance of LSM-tree and outperforms state-of-the-art designs.

# A. Evaluation Setup

**Summary:** The partial document discusses the AisLSM system and its optimizations for handling compactions in LSM-trees using asynchronous I/O operations facilitated by io_uring. Key points include:

1. **Compaction Process**: AisLSM uses io_uring structures to manage data for SST files and employs asynchronous I/O operations to enhance compaction efficiency. It checks the durability of parental SST files and manages the deletion of grandparental files.

2. **Version and State Tracking**: AisLSM tracks changes in SST files using RocksDB's Manifest file and in-memory Version, decoupling visibility and durability for LnSST files.

3. **Concurrent Compactions**: The system supports concurrent compactions by utilizing multiple threads and the parallelism capabilities of modern CPUs and NVMe SSDs, enhancing performance without blocking user-space threads.

4. **I/O Polling and Error Handling**: AisLSM considers I/O polling with NVMe SSDs and handles I/O errors by deferring fsync checks, ensuring data durability even in case of errors.

5. **Outlier SST Files**: The system manages outlier SST files that are infrequently used, ensuring their durability and scheduling check-ups during off-peak hours.

6. **Evaluation Setup**: The document describes the evaluation platform, benchmarks, and competitors, highlighting AisLSM's performance improvements over other LSM-tree variants.

7. **Performance Analysis**: AisLSM significantly boosts performance by offloading I/O operations to kernel threads, reducing stall times, and achieving higher throughput compared to other state-of-the-art LSM-tree variants. The system's asynchronous I/O model effectively reduces the performance penalty of compactions.

with key ranges overlapped for compaction. Figure 7 illus-
trates eight main steps with which AisLSM does with an com-
paction. In these steps, AisLSM uses the io uring’s structures
such as uring_queue to collect data for each SST file. It
calls io uring’s interfaces such as io_uring_prep_fsync
andio_uring_submit to prepare an asynchronous fsync
and submit an I/O request, respectively.
Deferred check-up and deletion. At the beginning of a
compaction, AisLSM checks if input parental SST files are
already durable ( 8). If so, it removes grandparental SST
files by inserting them into a collection vector that RocksDB
has managed for the purpose of deleting files. The check-up
does not cost much time. For example, in dealing with the
aforementioned test of putting 80GB of KV pairs, AisLSM
spent overall 749.1 seconds, out of which all check-up actions
cost about 0.01 ms. Such a time cost is negligible.
Version and state tracking. RocksDB has a Manifest file
with an in-memory Version to record the change of SST
files (see Figure 1). As AisLSM decouples the visibility and
durability for LnSST file ( n≥1), it tracks and updates the
state of each LnSST file in the Manifest file and Version.
B. Optimizations and Complements
Concurrent compactions. AisLSM maintains background
threads to do flush and compaction jobs. It makes com-
putations of current compaction thread execute on a CPU
core while a kernel thread of io uring is simultaneously
handling I/Os with storage for prior compaction, without
blocking the user-space compaction thread. Today multi-core
and many-core CPUs have gathered momentum. NVMe SSD
also contains numerous hardware queues for parallel I/O
streams [21, 36] while Linux kernel has blk-mq with multiple
software queues [20, 40]. AisLSM supports multiple threads or
instances concurrently conducting compaction jobs. Its asyn-
chronous I/O model, when deployed on multiple compaction
threads, can exploit the parallelism capabilities of both CPU
and storage for effectual concurrent executions.
I/O polling. NVMe SSD embraces much shorter access
latency than SATA SSDs. Many researchers have used the I/O
polling mechanism, instead of conventional I/O interrupts, to
interact with NVMe SSD [20, 21, 35]–[37]. In implementing
AisLSM, we also consider I/O polling with NVMe SSD
and io uring. Note that the joint setup of I/O polling and
iouring currently works only when a file is opened with the
ODIRECT flag, i.e., in the direct I/O mode [38].
Failed I/Os. I/O errors might take place over time. When an
I/O operation fails, the conventional synchronous I/O model
helps LSM-tree handle the error in a timely fashion. As
AisLSM waits for the completion signals of all asynchronous
file writes, any I/O error occurring at these writes can be
swiftly detected and processed like with conventional LSM-
tree. AisLSM defers the check-up of asynchronous fsync ,
so detecting and handling I/O errors for fsync are also
postponed. However, even if an I/O error happens in persisting
an SST file, the durability of KV pairs stored in the file is not
impaired since AisLSM has retained parental SST files untilthe check-up. Searching KV pairs in this file is also unaffected
since file system accommodates KV pairs in the OS’s buffer
cache or storage device’s disk cache. AisLSM explicitly calls
fsync for a retry to fix the I/O error. In the worst case, it
regenerates and replaces that problematic file.
Outlier SST files. In unusual cases, some SST files, once
generated in a compaction, hardly participate in subsequent
compactions, because the key ranges they cover might not
be frequently used (i.e., outliers). AisLSM still ensures the
durability of such inactive outlier SST files. This is the other
reason why AisLSM submits one request for all SST files
generated in a compaction to schedule a compound asyn-
chronous fsync . As long as any one of them is to be involved
in a future compaction, AisLSM checks if the asynchronous
fsync has been done for all relevant SST files. By doing
so, AisLSM avoids overlooking outliers. This also helps to
delete their parental SST files. In addition, there might be a
very low likelihood that outliers form a batch and have no
opportunity to be compacted again. AisLSM has tracked all
SST files asynchronously persisted with io uring. It schedules
a specific check-up in off-peak hours for such outliers.
VI. E VALUATION
A. Evaluation Setup
Platform. The machine used for evaluation is an HP Z2
G4 workstation. It is with an Intel Core i9-9900K CPU
and 64GB DRAM as main memory. The OS is Ubuntu
22.04.1 with Linux kernel 6.2.7 installed on an HDD (Western
WD20EZWX-60F5KA0 in 2TB). There are two additional
SSDs in the machine. One is an SATA SSD (Samsung 870
EVO in 1TB) and the other one is an NVMe SSD (SK
Hynix HFS512GD9TNGL2A0A in 480GB). The latter is used
as the main storage device to hold data for all LSM-tree
variants throughout following experiments. The compiler is
GCC/G++ version 9.5.0. The version of io uring (liburing) is
2.3. Because XFS and io uring have been jointly optimized
for efficient use of asynchronous I/Os [41, 42], we mainly use
XFS except for NobLSM that needs a customized Ext4.
Benchmarks. One benchmark we use is the db bench
micro-benchmark built in RocksDB. It can synthesize contin-
uous Put or Get requests in typical access patterns. The other
one is the YCSB macro-benchmark emulating a suite of real-
world workloads [43]. On finishing a workload, they report
the throughput (MB/s) or execution time that we utilize as the
metrics to measure and compare performances for LSM-trees.
Competitors. Besides the vanilla RocksDB [3], we choose
a few state-of-the-art LSM-tree variants that represent different
approaches researchers have explored to improve performance
for LSM-tree. They are ADOC [16], TRIAD [19], Rocks-
bu [31], SILK [12], PhotonDB [32] and NobLSM [26]. All
of them except NobLSM are open-source, implemented with
RocksDB. As to NobLSM built atop LevelDB, we implement
it by modifying RocksDB and Ext4 for a fair comparison. Be-
low we briefly summarize the characteristics of these variants.
ADOC. ADOC monitors the data flow among multiple
components of LSM-tree. Accordingly, it adjusts the numberof threads and size of SSTable to control processing rate and
schedule the frequency of background jobs, thereby in turn
controlling the data flow within LSM-tree to reduce stalls.
TRIAD. Firstly, TRIAD tries to separate hot KV pairs
that are frequently updated from cold ones at the memtable.
Secondly, TRIAD postpones a compaction until the overlap
between key ranges of SST files aggregates to some extent.
Thirdly, it makes use of WAL to play the role of L0SST file,
instead of writing the same KV pairs again. TRIAD attempts
to alleviate write amplification with these techniques.
Rocks-bu. Rocks-bu is the other RocksDB variant that we
have found being with the use of io uring. A team of three
practitioners made use of the batch I/O feature of io uring to
group I/O requests for RocksDB.
SILK. SILK focuses on I/O scheduling between insertions
with memtable, flushes, and compactions, mainly for shorter
tail latency. It allocates more bandwidth to internal operations,
i.e., flushes and compactions, when foreground service is not
heavy. It gives higher priority to flushes and compactions at
lower levels (e.g., L0→L1). Moreover, it allows compactions
at lower levels to preempt ones at higher levels.
PhotonDB. A group of Alibaba’s researchers engineered
PhotonDB by using io uring and coroutines to subsume
threads in RocksDB [44]. Although they have been aware
of asynchronous I/Os provided by io uring, they focus on
applying coroutines and io uring to serve multiple clients in a
network database. With a single client carrying one or multiple
foreground threads, PhotonDB still waits for the completion
of I/Os with io uring in the conventional synchronous manner.
NobLSM. NobLSM employs the periodical asynchronous
commit of Ext4 journaling to persist files and thus remove
fsync s out of the critical path of compaction. It relies on
Ext4 and demands handcrafted changes into Linux kernel.
B. Micro-benchmark
We employ db bench to issue four typical workloads. In
particular, with each LSM-tree variant, we perform following
workloads in order: fillrandom (random insertion of KV pair),
overwrite (random update of KV pair), readseq (sequential
retrieval of KV pair), and readrandom (random retrieval of
KV pair). For each workload, we fix an overall quantity of
data volume and follow the default uniform distribution to
generate requests. We designate four foreground threads. Each
thread puts (resp. gets) 20GB of KV pairs for write (resp. read)
requests. We set the key size as 16B while varying the value
size to be 64B, 128B, 256B, 512B, 1KB, 2KB, and 4KB. The
reason we use 80GB of data is twofold. Firstly, such a volume
of data concretely entails continual compactions with massive
CPU computations and disk I/Os over time. Secondly, the
NVMe SSD we are running on has 480GB raw capacity. We
must consider LSM-tree’s write amplifications that can occupy
multiple times of 80GB [13, 19, 27, 45]–[47]. We also take
into account that due to a composition of LSM-tree variants,
workloads, value sizes, and rounds, overwhelming data may
frequently trigger SSD’s internal modules like garbage collec-tion and wear leveling that impact performance results [48]–
[50]. We choose a volume of 80GB to alleviate such impact.
Figure 8a to Figure 8d capture the bandwidth of each LSM-
tree variant with four workloads. Let us analyze the results
in three aspects. Firstly, using its asynchronous I/O model
to revolutionize compaction, AisLSM significantly boosts the
performance of RocksDB. For example, with fillrandom and
seven increasing value sizes, the throughput of AisLSM is
1.3×, 1.4×, 1.6×, 1.8×, 2.0×, 2.1×, and 2.14 ×that of
RocksDB. As AisLSM offloads file write and fsync I/Os
to kernel threads and makes compaction thread focus on CPU
computations, it is able to quickly complete a compaction job
and soon initiate the next one, thereby gaining high through-
put. We have further recorded the stall time for AisLSM.
As mentioned in Section III, RocksDB spent 1,399.9 seconds
in finishing fillrandom with 1KB values while stalls lasted
for 1,179.1 seconds. For AisLSM, the total execution time
and stall time are 749.1 and 618.1 seconds, respectively. This
comparison further justifies that the removal of synchronous
I/Os from the critical path of compaction effectually reduces
the stall time and in turn boosts performance for LSM-tree.
In addition, given a fixed size of SST file (64MB), AisLSM
achieves higher performance with larger values. A larger value
size means fewer KV pairs to be fitted in an SST file. LSM-tree
starts off a compaction regarding the capacity of each level, or
measured in the practical unit, the number of SST files. With
the same number of SST files for compaction, fewer KV pairs
evidently need less time on merge-sorting keys and other CPU
computations. As a result, AisLSM finishes a compaction in
a more prompt pace for larger KV pairs.
Secondly, AisLSM significantly outperforms state-of-the-
art prior works. For example, with overwrite workload and
1KB values, the throughput of AisLSM is 1.8 ×, 2.0×, 2.9×,
1.9×, 2.3×, 1.6×, and 1.4 ×that of original RocksDB, ADOC,
TRIAD, Rocks-bu, SILK, PhotonDB and NobLSM, respec-
tively. These LSM-tree variants have undertaken different
approaches to optimize LSM-tree, mainly on reducing the
performance penalty caused by compactions. ADOC and SILK
take into account the processing capability of storage device
and attempt to schedule compaction jobs with threads. Simi-
larly, one main technique of TRIAD is to postpone scheduling
compactions until it has to do so due to too many overlapped
keys. Whereas, they place emphasis on scheduling at the
granularity of compaction jobs but fail to realize the critical
serial order of CPU computations and storage I/Os in a com-
paction. Consequently, their compaction thread stays waiting
for I/O completion signals from kernel thread while CPU core
does not simultaneously work on meaningful computations.
Given a mass of KV pairs that are continuously arriving to
stress LSM-tree, the effect of scheduling compaction jobs is
inferior and unsatisfactory. As to PhotonDB and Rocks-bu, a
replacement over conventional concepts or interfaces without
an in-depth study to locate concrete performance bottlenecks
is unlikely to bring about substantial gains. Let us still take
overwrite and 1KB value size for example. With coroutine and

# B. Micro-benchmark

**Summary:** The partial document discusses various optimizations and enhancements to LSM-tree-based systems, particularly focusing on different variants of RocksDB. Key points include:

1. **TRIAD**: This approach separates frequently updated (hot) key-value pairs from less frequently updated (cold) ones, postpones compaction until necessary, and uses the Write-Ahead Log (WAL) to reduce write amplification.

2. **Rocks-bu**: Utilizes io_uring for batch I/O to improve RocksDB's performance.

3. **SILK**: Focuses on I/O scheduling to reduce tail latency by prioritizing internal operations like flushes and compactions when the system is not heavily loaded.

4. **PhotonDB**: Developed by Alibaba, it uses io_uring and coroutines to handle multiple clients, though it still relies on synchronous I/O for completion.

5. **NobLSM**: Uses asynchronous commit of Ext4 journaling to improve performance but requires changes to the Linux kernel.

6. **AisLSM**: This variant significantly boosts performance by using asynchronous I/O to handle compactions, reducing stall time, and improving throughput compared to other variants.

7. **Micro-benchmarking**: The document describes benchmarking using db_bench with various workloads and value sizes to evaluate the performance of these LSM-tree variants, highlighting AisLSM's superior performance in both write and read operations.

8. **Crash Consistency and Data Accessibility**: AisLSM is tested for crash consistency and data accessibility, showing it maintains data integrity and accessibility similar to RocksDB.

9. **Tail Latency**: The document also considers tail latency as a critical performance metric, especially for latency-sensitive applications.

workloads under three distributions, i.e., Zipfian, uniform, and
latest. Because of space limitation, we present the execution
time with workloads A and F, as both of them contain a
50%/50% mix of write and read requests. As indicated by Fig-
ure 13, AisLSM outperforms other LSM-tree variants under
Zipfian and uniform distributions. With the latest distribution,
AisLSM achieves a comparable performance than RocksDB.
The reason is that, the latest distribution always chooses the
most recent data for operation. Write and read requests are
hence mostly satisfied at LSM-tree’s memtables and block
cache. With regard to frequent merges upon updating the
same keys repeatedly at the memtable level, compactions are
not largely triggered. The performance gain of revolutionized
compaction is consequently marginal for AisLSM.
VII. R ELATED WORKS
We have quantitatively discussed and evaluated a few prior
works in Section VI. Some techniques of them have been
proved to be useful to reduce the performance penalty caused
by compactions. For example, the way TRIAD separates hot
and cold KV pairs was also considered by other works. Huang
et al. [27] found that even a small number of frequently
updated hot KV pairs would quickly fill up SST files and cause
more compaction jobs over time. They accordingly install an
auxiliary log to distinguish and handle hot data. Decoupling
values from keys is another technique that can effectively
lower the frequency of compactions, since a pointer (location)
of each actual value, instead of the entire value, is stored in
SST file [19, 28, 29]. Some researchers proposed concurrent
compactions [14, 30, 57]. For example, p2KVS [30] mentioned
in Section VI-C7 partitions KV space into independent spaces
and manages multiple instances correspondingly. Such in-
stances concurrently schedule and perform compaction jobs.
There are also research works that leverage buffers to acceler-
ate search performance for LSM-tree [51, 55]. AisLSM’s rev-
olutionized compaction is complementary to these techniques
and they can collaboratively take effect for high performance.
Foregoing designs mainly attempt at the granularity of
compaction jobs. Some researchers considered dissecting the
internals of a compaction. For example, Zhang et al. [17]
tried to make use of the parallelism between CPU and I/O
device, like what we have done in this paper. However, they
decomposed a compaction job in the granularity of blocks(4KB by default). Then they tried to pipeline CPU computation
and synchronous I/Os for consecutive blocks of every SST
file. Limited by the perspective at the block-level granularity
and obliviousness of asynchronous I/Os, they had to rely
on multiple parallel storage devices for high I/O bandwidth
to catch up the computing speed of CPU. Whereas, this
demands changes across user- and kernel-spaces for storage
management. Additionally, their pipeline might not be stable
over time, since small data in one or few blocks is difficult
for CPU and storage to process at a steadily stable speed.
Comparatively, AisLSM takes effect at the granularity of SST
file in scores of megabytes and exploits existing storage stack
(e.g., io uring and NVMe SSD) for implementation. It shall
have higher performance, viability, and stability.
Not many researchers considered the impact of fsync s
used in compactions on the performance of LSM-tree [25, 26].
Prior to aforementioned NobLSM, Kim et al. [25] proposed
BoLT. BoLT produces one huge output SST file for each
compaction and persists all compacted KV pars in one aggre-
gated fsync . This reduces the performance penalty caused by
multiple fsync calls on individual SST files, but the eventual
large fsync still synchronously occurs on the critical path.
Researchers also studied the processing speeds for compu-
tations and I/Os for compaction. Some of them used FPGA
to accelerate computations [58, 59]. The emerging storage
devices like NVMe SSD and persistent memory (pmem) also
attracted wide attention [20, 47, 60]. For example, Chen et
al. [20] proposed SpanDB that jointly makes use of faster
NVMe SSD and ordinary slower SSD to suit the characteristics
of WAL and SST files for storage. It also uses I/O polling
with NVMe SSD. In addition, SpanDB and p2KVS share
similarity in dedicating separate foreground and background
threads to serve user requests and do flush or compaction
jobs, respectively. By doing so, SpanDB aims to overlap fore-
ground services with background jobs at runtime. Meanwhile,
researchers developed LSM-tree variants [6, 7, 13, 14, 29, 61]
to leverage the non-volatility and byte-addressability of pmem.
Though, the winding down of Intel’s Optane DC memory
business [62, 63] may impact the deployment of them.
VIII. C ONCLUSION
In this paper, we overhaul the compaction procedure of
LSM-tree. The critical path of a compaction job is composed
of CPU computations and disk I/Os. At runtime, LSM-tree’s
compaction thread synchronously waits for the completion of
file write and fsync I/Os that a kernel thread is handling. We
accordingly develop AisLSM that overlaps CPU computations
(resp. user thread) with disk I/Os (resp. kernel thread) for
consecutive compactions and, particularly, performs disk I/Os
with an asynchronous model. AisLSM also decouples the
visibility from durability for compacted KV pairs. With a
deferred check-up and deletion strategy, AisLSM ensures that
data stored in SST files is visible and durable. We thoroughly
evaluate AisLSM. Experiments show that, by shortening the
critical path of compaction, AisLSM highly boosts the perfor-
mance of LSM-tree and outperforms state-of-the-art designs.

**Summary:** The partial document discusses the performance evaluation and comparison of various Log-Structured Merge-tree (LSM-tree) variants under different data distributions, specifically focusing on workloads A and F, which have a balanced mix of read and write requests. AisLSM is highlighted as outperforming other LSM-tree variants under Zipfian and uniform distributions, while achieving comparable performance to RocksDB under the latest distribution. The document also reviews related works on optimizing LSM-tree performance, particularly focusing on techniques to reduce the performance penalty caused by compactions. These techniques include separating hot and cold key-value pairs, decoupling values from keys, and using concurrent compactions. The document further explores the impact of fsync operations on LSM-tree performance and discusses various approaches to improve compaction efficiency, such as using FPGA for computation acceleration and leveraging emerging storage technologies like NVMe SSDs. The conclusion emphasizes the development of AisLSM, which enhances LSM-tree performance by overlapping CPU computations with disk I/Os using an asynchronous model, and evaluates its effectiveness in boosting performance compared to state-of-the-art designs.
